title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: 28 officials targeted in recalls over data center votes—what it means for towns and bills.

lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Tonight we're digging into the growing recall pressure on local officials over data center decisions, plus fresh rejections, lawsuits, and power proposals from across the state.
Graham, that Bridge Michigan analysis from Friday really caught my eye—twenty-eight officials in eight communities facing recalls, and only one actually on the November ballot so far.

Exactly. These fights have been building for months as proposals pop up in rural townships and small cities, and residents are pushing back hard on the power demands, water use, and potential tax breaks.
Why do you think the recalls are landing now? Is it just the sheer number of projects, or something specific about how these votes are going down?
A bit of both. The analysis shows these efforts tied directly to data center votes, and with projects eyeing everything from farmland to existing dam sites, locals are organizing fast.
What does this mean for electric bills? We've heard concerns about rates spiking if these big users come online.

That's the core worry in places like Forsyth Township, where hundreds showed up Saturday to grill officials on exactly that—how new data centers could affect local electricity rates and water supplies.
And the military ties rumor there too? That added another layer.
It did. Residents wanted straight answers on power and water, plus any rumored military connections near the Marquette County sites.
Shifting to western Michigan, South Haven neighbors are fighting a rezoning on Baseline property over noise, traffic, and strain on services. How does that fit the bigger pattern?
It's the same story playing out in multiple townships—pushback that could set the tone for nearby communities if the rezoning fails or succeeds.
And the Kluver Road project in another township got rejected outright on Saturday for those exact resident concerns about noise, traffic, and water.
Right, that decision keeps the rural area free of large-scale server farms for now, but developers are already testing other spots.
What about the developer suing Gibraltar to overturn the year-long moratorium? That feels like a direct test of local power.
It is. The firm claims the pause illegally blocked their project, and if they win, Wayne County residents near the site could see delayed tax revenue and jobs.
Meanwhile, St. Joseph County is weighing its own two-year freeze while they study roads, water, and electricity impacts.
Residents there are worried about higher utility bills and lost farmland, and whatever they decide could influence other southwest Michigan townships.
In Saline, dozens packed a coffee hour Friday to question leaders on power costs, water use, and lost tax revenue if projects get breaks.
That session showed how fast this is becoming a flashpoint in Washtenaw County.
And the Mason project finally named its developer on Friday, giving Ingham County residents a clearer target for questions on water, noise, and grid impact.
Transparency helps, but it also means more organized opposition is likely.
Then there's Hyperscale Data selling forty-three million dollars in Bitcoin to fund their Michigan push, cutting debt and earmarking cash for buildout.
Crypto volatility directly funding local infrastructure plans—residents will feel it through added power demand and potential tax deals.
And the GenH pitch today using the existing Morley Dam site in Mecosta County for a self-generating data center—could that sidestep some utility fights?
It might, but it still raises the same questions about water use and local impacts, and how the project gets classified under state rules.
So with all these fronts, Graham, what's the bigger picture for what happens next with these recalls?
The one recall already on the ballot could be a bellwether, and more petitions are circulating in communities where votes went against resident concerns.
How many townships have already paused projects while they study this?
At least a handful like St. Joseph and Gibraltar, and the pattern suggests others will follow as the power and water questions get louder.
What does a typical data center actually pull in terms of power? Enough to affect residential rates?
These facilities are massive users, and that's exactly why residents from Saline to Forsyth are asking officials for hard numbers before approvals move forward.
And farmland loss—how much is at stake in these rural fights?
Proposals often target open land, which is why groups are organizing around preserving it and protecting local services.
If recalls start succeeding, could that slow the overall buildout or just push projects to more willing communities?
It could do both—slow things in hot spots while developers shop around for places with fewer hurdles.
The Gibraltar lawsuit outcome will be key there too.
Absolutely—it tests how far locals can go to pause these facilities.
Shifting to tomorrow's calendar, what's on deck for listeners who want to show up?
Monday the Planning Commission reviews a new site plan application for the Verrus data center project.
That sounds like a chance for direct input on one of these proposals.
It is—agendas like that are where residents can ask the specific questions we've been talking about all show.
Any other quick context on how these meetings usually go?
They often draw packed rooms when data centers are on the agenda, with folks focusing on power, water, and traffic just like in Saline and Forsyth this week.
Graham, wrapping the big picture, do you see the recall pressure changing how officials vote going forward?
It already is in some places—officials are facing real accountability, and that could lead to more studies and pauses before approvals.
And for the projects that do move ahead, like the one with the named developer in Mason, what should neighbors watch?
The details on tax deals, water agreements, and grid connections—those are the parts that hit local bills and services hardest.
The GenH dam idea today feels like a creative workaround, but still brings the same water questions.
Right, and how it's classified could determine whether it faces the full utility review or not.
With the Bitcoin sale funding one push and the lawsuit testing another, the industry is adapting fast.
And communities are adapting too—organizing recalls, packing meetings, and demanding answers.
So the story isn't slowing down anytime soon.
Not with new proposals and pushback hitting almost every region we covered.
Thanks for walking through the stakes, Graham. Listeners, stay tuned for those meetings if you're nearby.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Recall Heat on Officials as Data Center Fights Spread Across Michigan
